scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: I'm covering the monitoring desk today. An alert
popped up in the night and then cleared itself, and the ops chat is clear
about what it was: one of the big middle routers -- they keep writing "R6",
one message says maybe "R7" -- crashed, and everything going through the
middle is falling into a hole. Half the screens look normal to me, but I am
not going to second-guess the ops people, and I've been told to get this
looked at urgently. So: one of your middle boxes died. Check it and sort it
out today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
A thorough inspection of every device in the Kath5 topology — with particular attention to R6 and R7 as flagged by the ops team — reveals no active fault. Both routers are completely healthy: their FRR stacks (zebra, ospfd, watchfrr) started normally at 20:10, and all OSPF adjacencies converged within one minute of startup and have remained in Full state ever since. R6 holds three Full neighbours (R4 via segment S, R5 via segment V, R7 via segment Y), and R7 holds one Full neighbour (R6 via segment Y). Routing tables on both are complete, carrying inter-area summaries for all five OSPF areas (0–4) as well as redistributed EIGRP prefixes from the R11/R12 edge domain.

Broader network health is equally clean: the R4–R8 virtual link (bridging Area 2 to Area 0 through Area 1) is Full, R11's EIGRP peerings with R12 and R13 are active, and data-plane reachability through the mid-network zone — pinged from both PC0 (Area 0) and R9 to R6's and R7's interfaces and stub prefixes (60.x, 67.x, 70.x, 80.x) — returns 0% loss across the board.

The monitoring alert the ops team observed almost certainly reflects normal OSPF convergence noise immediately after the lab container stack was started: with a cold-start at 20:10, the protocol needs roughly 60 seconds to elect DRs and exchange LSAs, during which a monitoring probe to Area 1 destinations would time out. Watchfrr did not log any daemon crash or restart. There is no injected or configuration fault to remediate. The correct action is to mark the alert as a false positive and confirm with the monitoring team that convergence-window alerts should be suppressed for a short hold-down period after a scheduled lab restart.

per_axis.axis: bonus-notes-baseline-healthy: notes R6/R7 are up (ospfd running, R6<->R7 adjacency Full) and PC0 reaches PC12 across the core at baseline
per_axis.rationale: While the writeup confirms R6/R7 are up with OSPF adjacency Full, it never explicitly demonstrates end-to-end reachability from PC0 to PC12 (PC0→PC12) as required.

The agent's investigation log shows concrete checks of FRR processes, OSPF neighbor states across routers, FRR logs, and an end-to-end reachability test (PC0→PC12) that returned 0% loss; the writeup draws logical, supported inferences that the reported crash is not reproducible and that the alert was likely convergence noise. A few detailed claims (exact route/area summaries counts) are restatements beyond truncated outputs but overall the evidence in the log supports the conclusion.
